correctness.rationale: Total vertex-edge domination of D is equivalent to the complement of N[D] containing no edge (N[D] is a vertex cover) together with G[D] having no isolated selected vertices. All one-/two-vertex sets fail totality, except an adjacent pair {a_i,b_j} with i!=j, and that pair leaves the genuine edge a_j b_i outside N[D], so gamma>=3. A total three-set must have two vertices on one shore and one opposite; every one of its two same-shore vertices must see the lone opposite vertex, forcing three distinct matching indices. Each such triple covers all opposite vertices and all but potentially one same-shore vertex by N[D], hence is VE-dominating. Two orientations yield exactly n(n-1)(n-2) minima for all n>=3. Independent subset-level exhaustions for 3<=n<=8 reproduce the complete family.
residual_risks: Only standard total vertex-edge domination defined via closed-neighborhood coverage; not standard total domination.
Arbitrary-n claim follows from vertex cover argument, finite checks corroborative only.

value.rationale: The invariant is defined and motivated in graph domination theory; removal of a perfect matching from a biclique provably raises its total vertex-edge minimum from 2 to 3, and ALL minimum three-vertex witnesses are classified by distinct matching indices. The closed formula n(n-1)(n-2) is a complete natural infinite-family census, not just a test case or renaming.
residual_risks: Elementary breadth and no arbitrary matching-deletion extension.

limitations: Connected balanced crowns n>=3, not arbitrary K_{p,q} minus a matching.
